solution:
Low.
Slanting sunrays and melting snow describe the temperate region. Because the sunrays fall slanting here, the temperature is lower and the rate of evaporation is small. At the same time the melting of snow adds a large supply of freshwater to the sea. Since the supply of freshwater exceeds the rate of evaporation, the salinity is low; the chapter's table gives the average salinity of the temperate region (35° to 65°) as 33‰.

Medium.
A cloudy sky with rainfall through the year describes the equatorial calm belt. Here the sky stays cloudy for long periods and convectional rainfall occurs every day, and large rivers like the Congo and the Amazon meet the sea, so the supply of freshwater is abundant and this pulls the salinity down. But the temperature in this belt is high, so the rate of evaporation is also high, which keeps the salinity from falling very low. The two effects balance each other and the chapter's table gives the average salinity of the equatorial region (0° to 15°) as 34‰, which is less than the tropical 37‰ but more than the temperate 33‰.

High.
Clear skies for most of the year and perpendicular sunrays describe the tropical zone. Perpendicular sunrays and a cloudless sky mean the temperature is high, so the rate of evaporation is high. Evaporated water leaves the sea as water vapour but the amount of salt in the remaining water stays the same, so the salinity rises. Clear skies also mean little rainfall, so the supply of freshwater is small. The chapter's table gives the average salinity of the tropical region (15° to 35°) as 37‰, the highest of the four latitudinal zones.

High.
A desert area around the sea means very little rainfall and almost no supply of freshwater from rivers, while the heat of the desert keeps the rate of evaporation very high. Where the rate of evaporation is greater than the supply of freshwater, the salinity is high. This is why the seas of the mid-latitudinal zone (25° to 35° N and S), which holds the hot deserts of the world, are highly saline, and why the Dead Sea, which has low rainfall, a low supply of freshwater and high evaporation, reaches a salinity of 332‰ against the ocean average of 35‰.

Low.
Low temperatures mean the rate of evaporation is very small, so little water leaves the sea as vapour and the salts stay diluted. An ample supply of river water at the same time keeps adding freshwater to the sea. Since the supply of freshwater exceeds the rate of evaporation, the salinity is low. The chapter's table gives the average salinity of the polar region (65° to 90°) as 31‰, the lowest of the four latitudinal zones, and the land-locked Baltic Sea only 7‰.

High.
A continental location means the sea is land-locked. Land-locked seas have higher salinity than open seas, because the rate of evaporation is more and there is a lack of supply of freshwater from large rivers. A desert around and low rainfall make both of these worse, as there is almost no rain and almost no river water to replace what evaporates. The chapter's figures show this clearly: the land-locked Mediterranean Sea has 39‰ and the Red Sea 41‰, against 35‰ for the Atlantic Ocean, while the Dead Sea reaches 332‰, the Great Salt Lake 220‰ and the Caspian Sea 155‰.

The general rule of the chapter is that in seas where the supply of freshwater exceeds the rate of evaporation, the salinity is low. The Baltic Sea lies in a cold region, so its temperature is low and very little of its water is lost by evaporation. Against this small loss it keeps receiving a large supply of freshwater from rivers and from melting snow, and because the sea is land-locked this freshwater collects in it instead of mixing away into the open ocean. The chapter's table therefore shows the Baltic Sea with an average salinity of only 7‰, far below the ocean average of 35‰. The Baltic is thus an exception to the usual rule that land-locked seas are more saline than open seas, because there the supply of freshwater, not evaporation, is the stronger factor.
[Note: the chapter does not describe the Baltic Sea in its prose; it gives only its average salinity of 7‰ in the table of land-locked seas, so the reason above is the chapter's general rule applied to that figure.]

The Red Sea is a land-locked sea, and the chapter's table gives its average salinity as 41‰, well above the ocean average of 35‰. Salinity is high wherever the rate of evaporation is greater than the supply of freshwater. The northern part of the sea is shut in by desert land, so it gets very little rainfall and almost no river water, while the heat keeps evaporation very high; the salinity there is therefore higher. The southern part lies towards the opening of the sea, where the exchange of water with the ocean and a comparatively better supply of freshwater keep the salinity lower. So the difference between the two ends is caused by the difference in the supply of freshwater against the rate of evaporation.
[Note: the chapter does not describe the northern and southern parts of the Red Sea separately; it gives only the sea's average salinity of 41‰, so the reason above is the chapter's general rule applied to the two parts.]

Latitude is not the only factor that decides salinity. Salinity depends on the balance between the rate of evaporation and the supply of freshwater, and this supply is uneven from place to place, so two seas at the same latitude can differ. A land-locked sea has a higher salinity than an open sea at the same latitude, because its rate of evaporation is more and it lacks a supply of freshwater from large rivers: the average salinity of the Mediterranean Sea is 39‰, while that of the Atlantic Ocean, the most saline ocean, is 35‰. The same is seen on either side of India, where the salinity of the eastern coast is 34‰ while that of the Arabian Sea on the west is 35‰. Rainfall, the number of large rivers meeting the sea, and whether the sea is open or enclosed therefore make oceans at the same latitude differ in salinity.

The heat of the sea water comes from the sun. Most of the sunrays radiate back from the surface of the sea and only some of them penetrate to a certain depth, so the intensity of the sunrays goes on decreasing as the depth increases. Since less and less heat reaches the deeper water, the temperature keeps falling with depth. This fall continues only up to a depth of 2000 m. After 2000 m the temperature of the sea water is uniform everywhere, about 4°C from the equatorial regions right up to the polar areas, because sunrays, winds and currents no longer reach that far down to change it. The temperature reduces only up to 4°C with depth, and that is why the water at greater depths does not freeze.

We obtain salt from salt-pans, in which sea water is allowed to evaporate so that the salt dissolved in it is left behind. The more saline the sea water is, the more salt is obtained from the same quantity of water, so salt-pans are made where the salinity is higher. India has the Arabian Sea to its west and the Bay of Bengal to its east, and the chapter gives the salinity of the eastern coast as 34‰ while that of the Arabian Sea is 35‰. Because the water of the western coast is more saline than that of the eastern coast, salt-pans are more numerous on the western coast of India.
[Note: the chapter gives these two figures but leaves the reason for the higher salinity of the western coastal region as a question for the student; it does not state that reason itself.]

In the mid-latitudinal zones, that is between 25° and 35° north and south of the equator, rainfall is less and the supply of freshwater coming from rivers is also low. The hot deserts of the world lie in this zone, so the temperature is high and the rate of evaporation is high as well. Water keeps leaving the sea as vapour while the amount of salt in the remaining water stays the same, and very little freshwater comes in to replace what has evaporated. Because the rate of evaporation is greater than the supply of freshwater, the salinity of the seas is found to be higher in this zone; the chapter's table gives the average salinity of the tropical belt (15° to 35°) as 37‰, the highest of the four latitudinal zones.

The salinity of sea water is decided mainly by the balance between the rate of evaporation and the supply of freshwater. Where the rate of evaporation is higher than the supply of freshwater, the salinity is high; where the supply of freshwater exceeds the rate of evaporation, the salinity is low; and where both the supply of freshwater and the evaporation are low, the salinity is not affected much. The uneven distribution of temperature on the earth is therefore a factor, because a higher temperature means faster evaporation, as in the tropical zone where the salinity is high, while in the polar areas the temperature is very low, evaporation is very less and the salinity is low. Latitude works through this, as the sunrays are perpendicular near the equator and slanting in the temperate region. The uneven supply of freshwater is the second factor, and it depends on rainfall, on the large rivers that meet the sea, and on the water added by melting snow. Lastly, whether a sea is open or land-locked matters: land-locked seas have higher salinity than open seas because their rate of evaporation is more and they lack a supply of freshwater from large rivers, which is why the Mediterranean Sea has 39‰ against the Atlantic Ocean's 35‰.

Salinity is high in the belts on either side of the equator that fall in the tropical and mid-latitudinal zone. In this zone, between 25° and 35° north and south of the equator, rainfall is less and the supply of freshwater from rivers is also low, and the hot deserts of the world lie here. The temperature is high, so the rate of evaporation is high, while very little freshwater comes in to replace the water lost as vapour. As the rate of evaporation is greater than the supply of freshwater, the salinity of the seas is higher here than anywhere else. The chapter's table gives the average salinity of the tropical belt (15° to 35°) as 37‰, against 34‰ in the equatorial region, 33‰ in the temperate region and 31‰ in the polar region. Going away from this belt towards the poles, the sunrays become slanting, the temperature falls, melting snow adds more freshwater, and so the salinity decreases with increasing latitude.
[Note: the chapter does not use the names Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn and does not give their latitude; it describes this belt as the tropical zone (15° to 35°) and the mid-latitudinal zone (25° to 35° N and S).]

The surface temperature of sea water is not uniform everywhere and depends on several factors. The first is latitude: the surface temperature decreases from the equatorial areas towards the poles, the average being around 25°C in the equatorial areas, 16°C in the mid-latitudes and about 2°C near the poles. The second is depth, because most of the sunrays radiate back from the surface and their intensity decreases as the depth increases, so the temperature falls up to 2000 m and then stays at about 4°C everywhere. Ocean currents are a third factor: where cold ocean currents flow the surface temperature is less, and where warm currents move the temperature increases. Besides these, cyclones, rainfall, sea waves, salinity, pollution, convectional currents and the seasons also affect the surface temperature. Finally, there is a difference between open and land-locked seas, for as the salinity of land-locked seas is more, their temperature is higher than that of the open seas in the low latitudinal areas.

Most of the sunrays radiate back from the surface of the sea and only some of them penetrate to a certain depth, so the intensity of the sunrays decreases as the depth increases and the temperature of the sea water falls with depth. The change is greatest near the surface: the sea water up to a depth of about 500 m is called surface water, and it is this water that is affected by the sunrays and the ocean currents, so the change in temperature is fastest here. The temperature keeps decreasing up to a depth of 2000 m. After 2000 m the temperature is uniform everywhere, about 4°C from the equatorial regions to the polar areas, because at greater depths winds, sunrays and currents do not reach to change it; the chapter's graph of temperature, salinity and density shows that below about 1000 m there is almost no change in these factors. The temperature reduces only up to 4°C with depth, so the water at greater depths does not freeze. The fall with depth is not the same everywhere: the temperature of the sea water changes rapidly with depth in the equatorial areas, while in the polar areas the difference is lesser, because the surface water there is already cold.

The factors affecting salinity are: the rate of evaporation of sea water; the supply of freshwater to the sea, through rainfall, river water and melting snow; the temperature of the water, and with it the latitude, since temperature is unevenly distributed over the earth; and whether the sea is open or land-locked.

Temperature and salinity are the two properties of sea water that control its density. If the temperature reduces, the density of the water increases, because cold water is denser. Of the two, temperature affects the density more than salinity does. This is why sea water that is more saline but has a lower temperature at the surface still has a density greater than other water, while sea water having a higher temperature and low salinity can have a lower density.

Temperature decides how fast sea water evaporates, and evaporation decides the salinity. Where the temperature is high, evaporation happens at a faster rate; the evaporated water turns into water vapour and the quantity of water reduces, but the amount of salt in the remaining water stays the same, so the salinity increases. This is why in the tropical zone, where the temperature is higher and the rate of evaporation is also higher, the salinity is higher, and why the land-locked seas of desert regions such as the Dead Sea reach a salinity as high as 332‰. Where the temperature is low, the opposite happens: in the polar areas the temperature is very low, evaporation is very less, and so the salinity is low. In the temperate region too the sunrays are slanting and the temperature is lower, and along with the freshwater from melting snow this makes the salinity decrease as the latitude increases.
